425df0f734:
This chapter is about what an architect does before any architecture. You turn a business complaint into a problem statement with an owner, a pillar, a metric and a baseline. You write the constraints on one card. You test whether a language model belongs in the solution at all.

Then you prove feasibility per segment, with enough cases to mean something. You build a unit-economics model that includes the cost of wrong answers, and you check the design against latency, peak-volume and budget limits. You decide how much of the work is code and how much is Claude. Finally, you record the decision so a finance reviewer, a security reviewer and the next engineer can all follow it.

Every number in this chapter comes from a runnable example in the companion folder.
513f447619:
The item count, duration, fee, score scale and domain weights repeated in this guide are unverified. They come from secondary summaries, and Anthropic's public certification overview does not confirm them. The 95-percent-per-type question is a practice scenario written for this guide, not an official exam item.

For exam logistics and weighting, use the current Partner Academy candidate guide. The engineering lessons in this chapter don't depend on any of those exam facts.
ed926a4db1:
The whole chapter fits in two sentences.

A Claude solution starts as four written numbers, not as a diagram: the outcome with its metric, the baseline measured today, the constraints that cannot move (latency, compliance, budget, integration), and the cost of a wrong output.

Every later choice, whether to use a model at all, which tier, how many calls, how much human review, which pattern, is derived from those numbers and defended with arithmetic against them, per segment, in the form the requirement was written.
f25b2ec244:
Everything else follows from that. Each tool in this chapter exists to answer one specific failure:

The value pillars tell you which metric to measure and which trade you are allowed to make. The requirements card keeps the metric, the baseline and the constraints in one versioned place. The cost model, the evaluation gate and the architecture decision record all read from it.

The fit test exists because the cheapest, fastest and most accurate answer to some problems is a SQL query. The feasibility probe and the sample-size calculation exist because a demo that works on twenty curated examples tells you nothing about a threshold that must hold on every fallout code.

The ROI model includes the cost of errors, because a cheap wrong answer is expensive. The latency and capacity checks exist because the best design on paper can miss a p95 target by a factor of three. Example 06 shows that in a few seconds of simulation. And the hybrid split exists because arithmetic, limits and writes belong to code that behaves the same way every time.
9d8849fa47:
CCAR-P is the professional-level exam, and it asks a different kind of question from the foundations exam.

A foundations question checks whether you know the mechanism: which field ends a loop, which setting forces a tool call. A professional question describes a business situation, with figures, and offers four designs that all sound reasonable. You pick the one that meets the stated constraints at the lowest complexity. And you can say why the others fail. This one breaks the SLA. That one hides a failing segment behind an average. Another spends money on accuracy nobody asked for. Another puts a write behind no gate.

Get into the habit of putting numbers next to every option, and most of these questions answer themselves. This chapter builds that habit on one running example: a telecom BYOD (bring your own device) activation fallout queue, with a retail returns case alongside it.
f8ee27fc5a:
A note on scope. This chapter stops where chapter 02 begins. It decides whether and how much model to use, not which orchestration pattern to draw.

Other chapters own the deep treatments. Chapter 11 owns evaluation methodology (graders, datasets, A/B tests). Chapter 13 owns guardrails and human-in-the-loop design. Chapter 14 owns the compliance regimes. Here you meet only enough of each to make a launch decision. So when this chapter says a write needs a gate, or a field is regulated, read it as a pointer, not the full story.
6dc77c1539:
Nothing in this chapter is new to software architecture. That's why a senior Spring architect already has most of the instincts. What is new is the component itself: it has a statistical error rate and a per-token price.

The discipline around it was assembled from four older ones. It helps to know which piece of today's practice answers which old failure.
35d42b5b5c:
The software crisis of the late 1960s left two lasting habits.

The first was writing requirements down before building. IEEE Std 830 (first issued in 1984, revised in 1998) described what a good software requirements specification contains, and ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 later replaced it. The key idea was that a requirement must be verifiable. "The system shall be fast" is not a requirement. "95 percent of requests complete in under two seconds under 500 concurrent users" is.

The second habit was the feasibility study, with its three classic questions. Is it technically possible? Is it economically worthwhile? Can the organisation operate it? Those three questions come back almost unchanged in section 09, because they are still the right three.
0f068b70fe:
These practices solved one failure: the project that was never defined well enough to be judged. They did not anticipate a component whose behaviour is probabilistic.

A 1980s requirement could say "the lookup returns the balance" and test it with one case. A requirement on a language model has to say something like "the cause classifier is correct on at least 95 percent of cases in every fallout code, measured on a stratified sample of this size". One case proves nothing, and an average hides the weak segment.
038903432f:
Finance contributed the language stakeholders use to approve spending: net present value, payback period, sensitivity analysis. Consider a business case that says "the project returns 1.5 months of payback if wrong-remediation stays at one percent, and 6 months if it doubles". That is a capital-budgeting argument, and it's the argument sections 11 and 12 build.

Data science contributed CRISP-DM (published around 1999 and 2000). Its first phase was Business Understanding and its second was Data Understanding. In other words: before modelling, define the objective in business terms and look at the data you actually have. Teams that skipped those phases built models for the wrong target. The LLM-era version of the same mistake is the demo built before anyone measured the baseline.
c27122ae6c:
Site reliability engineering gave us the vocabulary of service level indicators, objectives and agreements, and the insistence on percentiles over averages. The p95 and p99 you'll quote against an SLA in section 13 come from that tradition.

Google's published "Rules of Machine Learning" opens with advice that the fit test in section 08 echoes: don't be afraid to launch a product without machine learning. A heuristic gets you most of the way, and it gives you data.

Then there's the 2015 paper "Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems" (Sculley and colleagues). It argued that the model is a small part of the system. Data dependencies, configuration, monitoring and glue code carry most of the cost. That is why this chapter prices the fixed operating cost along with the tokens.
e50221317d:
Once large language models became easy to call, a demo took an afternoon. Many organisations ran dozens of pilots with no baseline, no per-segment threshold and no cost model.

Industry surveys regularly report that a large share of generative AI pilots never reach production, or never show a measurable return. The exact percentages vary by survey, and I wouldn't quote any of them in a design review. But the pattern behind the reports is consistent, and it's the one this chapter is built to avoid. The pilot proved that the model can produce a plausible output. Nobody had written down what number would make the project worth running.

The CCAR-P blueprint's emphasis on "translating business problems into Claude solutions", aligned to value pillars, is that correction written into an exam.
37eb154e34:
Strip away the novelty, and a Claude call is a remote service with three properties an architect already knows how to reason about.

First, it has a unit cost that scales with tokens in and tokens out, not with requests. A 40,000-token contract review costs about a hundred times a 400-token classification on the same model.

Second, it has an error rate that is non-zero, task-dependent and silent. The failure is usually a plausible wrong answer, not a 500. So you can only find it by evaluating against known outcomes, never by a status code.

Third, it has a latency profile driven by two things: the number of output tokens and the number of sequential calls. A single call that writes six hundred tokens at a plausible 60 tokens per second spends about ten seconds generating. A six-call agent loop multiplies that floor by six.
162ba2782f:
A Spring architect sizing a new microservice asks four questions. What is the throughput? What is the p95? What does a failure cost? What does it cost to run? The same four apply here, with one addition, and the addition drives most of the design decisions in this domain: what does a wrong answer cost, and who catches it?

If the answer is "a few cents, and a reviewer sees it before it matters", you can automate aggressively. If it's "a wrong IMEI binding activates the wrong device and the customer's service stops", you add a gate. If it's "an unlawful disclosure of customer proprietary network information", you redesign the system so the model never sees data it doesn't need. The exam builds many of its scenarios around that last case.
61468830e0:
Two things in those formulas deserve plain words.

First, k, the number of calls per unit, is the lever that moves both cost and latency, and the pattern sets it. An augmented single call has k = 1. A workflow has a fixed, small k. An agent has a k that varies by case and has a long tail. Section 15 and chapter 02 come back to this.

Second, the error term is a rate multiplied by a cost, and at the start both are usually guesses. If the business case survives a threefold error in both guesses, it holds up. If it doesn't, it's a bet. Section 12 shows how to find out which one you have, in ten minutes.
2f6f416ff2:
Prices, rate limits, cache discounts and the batch discount all change. The examples in the companion folder take prices as parameters and use placeholders. For example: $3 and $15 per million input and output tokens for a mid tier, and one third of that for a small tier. Treat them as shapes, not quotes.

Before you put any dollar figure in front of a finance reviewer, check the docs for current prices. And write down in the document the date you took them.
0ecd132270:
The blueprint names five value pillars: efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, and performance against SLAs.

They are not marketing categories. Each one implies a different primary metric, a different baseline to collect, a different thing you may trade away, and a different way for the project to die. Name the pillar early, and you know what to measure and where the design has slack.
aebaf536df:
Most projects touch two or three pillars, but exactly one is primary. The primary pillar decides tie-breaks. If you keep one exam heuristic from this chapter, keep this one.

If the primary pillar is cost, a smaller model that clears the accuracy floor beats a larger one that exceeds it. If it's a performance SLA, you may pay more per call to meet p95, and a cheaper design that misses it is out, whatever its price. If it's efficiency, an extra review step that costs two minutes of a nine-minute task is probably wrong.

Watch for a common distractor: a design that improves a secondary pillar while harming the primary one. For example, a multi-agent system that raises accuracy by a point and triples latency, on a project whose primary pillar is the SLA.
5fa357495b:
Efficiency claims fail in review for one reason. Either the baseline was never collected, or it was collected from the wrong statistic.

Handle times are right-skewed. Most cases are routine, and a minority take far longer. That tail pulls the mean up, while the median describes the typical case. Example 12 builds a synthetic 90-day log of 123,000 fallout tickets and shows the gap.

Suppose your target is "9 minutes down to 4", the 9 was a median, and the finance model uses the mean. Then the savings are off by exactly that difference, in one direction or the other. Say which statistic you used. Section 07 shows the numbers.
432c3ff017:
The transformation pillar has no handle-time baseline, because the work wasn't being done at all. The value case rests on coverage, and on what the organisation does with the new signal.

Reading every care transcript instead of a one percent sample is only worth money if a retention team can act on what it finds. So the requirement you write is about that downstream action, not the number of transcripts read. For example: "a weekly list of the top 20 churn drivers per region delivered to retention, with at least 90 percent of listed drivers confirmed by a human spot check".

Two properties make these workloads attractive. Nobody waits for the output, so they're usually good batch candidates (section 14). And no customer-facing write happens, so the risk side is often low. That's why they tend to top portfolio rankings (section 18).
a780dd8c7d:
Generated code, documents and configuration still have to be reviewed. A tool that writes an integration adapter in six minutes, which then takes forty minutes to review and fix, has not improved productivity.

The metric is cycle time from ticket to merged and deployed change. The baseline is that cycle time before the tool, split by type of change. This pillar covers the developer-tooling material in chapter 17, and it often shows up as a team-level rollout decision rather than a service design.
1873f14db9:
Cost projects are the easiest to distort. The saving is easy to state: the outsourced queue costs $4.10 per ticket. The offsetting costs are spread out. There's rework when the automated answer is wrong, escalations that land on senior staff, customers who churn after a bad answer, and the fixed cost of evaluation and monitoring.

So a cost-pillar design is judged on total cost of ownership per resolved unit, with wrong outcomes priced in. In the exam's scenarios, the answer that quotes the lowest token price is often a distractor. The cheapest tier is only cheapest if it clears the threshold on every segment.
c5c5a5ee4d:
An SLA turns design choice into elimination. If the requirement is a draft within 20 seconds at p95 while an agent waits, then a design whose modelled p95 is 57 seconds is out. It doesn't matter how good its accuracy or net value is.

An SLA is not a weighting, and treating it like one is the usual mistake. "It's more accurate, so it's worth five more seconds" is acceptable only when the SLA leaves five seconds of room. Section 13 builds the p95 model that tells you how much room there is.
f80d97f7cf:
A requirements card is a one-page, versioned file that holds every number the design will be judged against.

It is short on purpose. Each field either constrains the architecture or defines how you'll prove value. A field with no consequence doesn't belong. In a Spring shop, think of it as a hybrid of a non-functional requirements sheet and the first page of a business case.

Why make it machine-readable instead of a slide? Because the same fields feed three other artefacts. The cost model reads volume, peak and budget. The evaluation gate reads thresholds and the segment key. The architecture decision record quotes the baseline, the constraints and the decision. When all three read one file, they can't disagree.
2ac8bf280d:
Three of those rows catch many design mistakes.

Acceptance thresholds are literal and per segment. In this guide's illustrative practice scenario, the requirement is 95 percent for each contract type, with an overall target of 96 percent. An aggregate 96 percent that hides one type at 91 percent fails. Measure each named segment, and fix any segment below its floor before launch. (This scenario is not an official exam item.) Write thresholds with the segment key named on the card.

Latency targets name a percentile. "Average under 10 seconds" is not something a user can feel. "p95 under 20 seconds" is.

The risk-of-wrong-output field converts an automation request into a design. "End to end autonomous agent" becomes "draft and approve" once that field says writes are high impact. Chapter 13 builds the gate.
2c157c4945: A card you can lint is a card people will keep honest. Example 01 loads card.json and rejects the five malformed variants a design review sees most often. It's twenty lines of code, and it catches exactly the omissions that later turn into disputes:
da311845e1:
Nobody hands you the card. The business sponsor describes a pain ("fallout is killing us"). The operations lead holds the data. The security reviewer holds the constraints. Finance holds the cost of a mistake.

Chapter 15 covers interview technique in depth. This section covers what you need to bring back from those conversations for this chapter's decisions. That matters for the exam, which often hides a missing number in the scenario and expects you to notice.
d9c21cb8c4:
Notice the pattern in the right-hand column. A missing number is not an obstacle. It's a task: measure it, bound it with a range, or choose the conservative default and write the assumption on the card. The failing move is to carry on with an unlabelled guess.

Mark every assumption on the card as an assumption, with an owner and a date by which a measurement will replace it. That's exactly the discipline shadow mode (section 17) supports.
c137cd241e:
One more piece of discovery matters for a professional-level answer: who the unit of work belongs to.

A fallout queue has an owner (Director, Order Operations). But the Kafka saga events belong to the platform team, the device registry to the device team, and the billing adjustments to a SOX-controlled finance system. Each owner has to agree to the integration surface and to the gates on writes.

A design that is perfect on paper, but that no team has agreed to expose, is not feasible. That's the operational-feasibility test in section 09.
cf33e049c4:
The baseline is the number that makes every later claim testable. It must be recent and sourced. It must be computed on the same unit as the target. And it must be broken down by the segments the threshold uses.

Example 12 builds a synthetic 90-day log of fallout tickets and computes the baseline the way a review would ask for it. The shapes are invented; the method is the point.
aa85b84306:
Three observations come out of that output.

First, the median is 9.0 minutes and the mean is 10.3, with a p95 of 21.3 minutes. The card says 9.0, so the card's baseline is a median. If the business case multiplies saved minutes by volume, it must use the median consistently, or explain why it uses the mean.

Second, the segments differ. Port-in cases take about 12 minutes at the median, the eSIM profile code 11, and the catch-all code 18. A flat "save 5 minutes per case" misses that the saving is largest where cases are longest. Those segments decide the total.

Third, the wrong-remediation rate is about 1.2 percent overall, but 1.8 percent in the tax-exempt code. With only 1,476 tickets in that code, the difference could be noise. That segment's baseline needs its own interval before anyone writes a segment-specific target.
c970015359:
An architect earns trust by saying "not an LLM" when that's the right answer. The exam rewards it too.

A language model is strong at a particular set of jobs:

  • understanding and producing unstructured language;
  • mapping messy input to structure;
  • reasoning over context supplied in the request;
  • handling the long tail of variation that rules can't enumerate.

It's a poor fit in five situations:

  • the logic is fully specified (a tax rate by state);
  • exact retrieval or arithmetic is the entire job (a balance for an account number);
  • the latency budget is below a model call's floor;
  • a large labelled set and a fixed label list make a trained classifier cheaper and faster;
  • a single error is unacceptable and can't be checked.

Each of those has a named alternative: rules or code, a database or API, classic machine learning, or a redesign that keeps a human decision.
f62ea403e7:
Read the last row of that output carefully. It's the one the exam likes. The store-hours chatbot is feasible, accurate and low-risk, and it still fails, on unit economics. It's worth less than it costs to run, and a static page solves the problem. A professional-level answer doesn't stop at "Claude can do it".

The row before it, auto-approving large goodwill credits, fails the catchability test. The problem isn't that the model is wrong too often. It's that nobody can cheaply tell when it is wrong. The fix is a redesign (a human decides, Claude drafts the justification), not a better prompt.
553b81b66c:
The strongest designs split a task by fit. In the fallout example it works like this. A deterministic lookup fetches the order, the device and the saga state. Claude reads the error payloads and the agent notes, classifies the cause and drafts the remediation. Code validates the remediation against business rules. A person approves the write. Each step uses the technology that is best at it.

So an exam option that sends everything through the model, eligibility rules and arithmetic included, is a distractor. Section 16 shows why with four runs. Three of them would have produced wrong output without a code-owned validator.
3a78d6c3fb:
The classic feasibility study has three parts. Each one can be tested in days, not quarters.

Technical feasibility asks whether the model can do the task to the threshold, on your data. You answer it with a stratified evaluation set built from real historical cases with known outcomes. Not curated examples.

Data feasibility asks whether the information the model needs is actually present, permitted and available at request time. Many failed pilots ask Claude to decide something that depends on data the integration never supplies.

Operational feasibility asks the people questions. Who reviews outputs? Who owns prompts? Who gets paged when quality drops? Will the owning teams expose the integration surface and accept the gates on writes?
b2ae8e7449:
You answer the technical question with a probe. Run a plain baseline prompt on the candidate tiers over a labelled sample. Report accuracy per segment, and record the average tokens per call.

One run gives two answers: whether the tier is viable, and what a call costs. Running two tiers shows early whether the cheaper one is good enough. Here is the core of example 03. Against the real API it uses anthropic.Anthropic(); offline it uses the scripted model in fallout.py:
961f0bbdd9:
The simulated model has a known true accuracy for each code, set in fallout.py. The small tier is genuinely weak on the promotion, plan-compatibility and catch-all codes. The mid tier is weak only on the catch-all.

Now look at what the probe did with thirty cases per code. It flagged eight codes for the small tier and three for the mid tier. But look at ADDR_VALID. The small tier's true accuracy there is 99 percent, yet the probe measured 90 percent, because three of thirty cases went the wrong way. That's not a bug. It's what 30 samples do, and the intervals printed beside it ([0.74, 0.97]) say so.

So the probe is a tool for locating where the work is, not for deciding launch. Two consequences follow. A code that looks bad at n=30 might be fine. And a code that looks perfect (IMEI_BLACKLIST at 30 of 30, interval 0.89 to 1.00) has not been shown to clear 95 percent. The next section turns this into a sample-size rule.
69c6a560f8:
"At least 95 percent in every segment" is a statistical claim, and a claim needs enough evidence.

Suppose a code has a true accuracy of exactly 95 percent. How many cases do you need to see before a run of results is unlikely to have come from that? With zero failures, the answer is 59. The chance of 59 straight successes at a true 95 percent rate is 0.95 to the 59th power, about 4.9 percent.

That's where the "rule of three" comes from: after n clean trials, the upper bound on the failure rate is roughly 3/n. And it's a minimum, because real systems do fail now and then. Allow one failure and the number is 93. Two failures, 124. Five failures, 208. Example 13 computes these exactly from the binomial distribution, using only the standard library.
d1e2920e2b:
Read the second table slowly.

A code with an observed accuracy of 97 percent, measured on 300 cases, has a Wilson lower bound of 0.944. Its point estimate is above the line, but it has not yet been shown to clear 95 percent with 95 percent confidence. At 600 cases it clears. The crossover is near 460, shown in FIG 8.

Multiply by fourteen codes and you can see the price of "per segment". Proving every code needs several thousand labelled cases. The rare codes cost months of data collection: a code with 0.4 percent of volume produces 164 tickets a month. That arithmetic sets up the three-state launch decision in section 17.
6af5549fc9:
This is where architects add judgement, and where the exam wants to see it.

A rare code with high risk and little volume should stay manual, because labelling it costs more than it's worth. A rare code with low risk can launch in shadow mode and build up evidence from production traffic. A high-volume code needs the full sample before the first automated draft.

Nothing in the threshold says all codes must launch together.
77abf1261f:
Stakeholders approve projects on money and risk. A credible model for a Claude solution has five parts:

  • the benefit per unit (labour minutes saved, valued at a fully loaded rate);
  • the volume;
  • the run cost per unit (tokens, from the formula in section 03);
  • the cost of errors (the change in error rate times the cost of one error);
  • the one-time build cost.

The error term is the one most often left out, and the one that most often decides the answer. A design that is cheap per call and wrong one percent of the time can wipe out the savings it creates.

The second most-omitted term is the fixed monthly operating cost: monitoring, evaluation upkeep, an on-call share. That's exactly what the 2015 paper on hidden technical debt was about.
0c275d9ac1:
Four designs, and one pattern worth reading closely.

Labour saved dominates every row: $5.10 per fallout, at 6.0 minutes saved at $0.85 a minute. Token cost is cents: 2 cents for a single call, 13 cents for a six-call agent loop with caching.

The agent loop wins on net value ($227k per month against $217k for the single call) only because of the error term. Lowering the wrong-remediation rate from 1.2 to 0.8 percent is worth $0.72 per unit at $180 per error. That beats the extra 11 cents of tokens.

That's the shape of justification the exam expects. The more expensive design can be right. But you have to defend it with a measured error reduction multiplied by what an error costs, not with an assumption that more steps mean more quality.
b573383140:
The fourth row is a failure the model catches early. The same agent loop with no prompt caching costs 29 cents per unit instead of 13. At three times peak volume, the run cost reaches $41,424, against a card that says $25,000.

So whether caching holds is a design decision with a dollar consequence, not a tuning detail. It depends on the stable prefix (system prompt, tool definitions, reference material) staying byte-identical across calls. Chapter 05 explains how to protect it.

The cache read multiplier of 0.1 used here is a placeholder. Check the docs for the current figure, and for the minimum cacheable prefix.
8890385008:
The second row surprises people. The cascade from a small tier to a mid tier has the lowest token cost (0.7 cents per unit), yet the lowest net value of the three real options ($182k a month). Why? The model assumes agents spend more time fixing the cheaper tier's drafts: 3.8 minutes against 3.0.

Saving $574 a month in tokens by paying $35k a month in labour is a bad trade. Whether that assumption holds is an empirical question, and shadow mode answers it (section 17). But the lesson stands. When labour is 40 times the token bill, optimise the quality of the draft, not the price of the call. Model selection is an economic decision before it's a technical one.
12774b458e:
In a Spring service, the token cost belongs next to the other per-request metrics, so finance and engineering read one number. A Micrometer counter tagged by use case and model lets you compare the measured cost per business unit against the ROI model every week. Example 15 does the same in Python (section 14).

The class below is the whole mechanism. Note that the prices come from configuration, not from constants.
56b0d6d595:
Every input to the ROI model is an estimate until shadow mode replaces it with a measurement. So don't argue about which estimate is right. Change them one at a time over a plausible range, and see which ones move the answer.

It takes ten minutes, and it tells you where to spend your measurement effort. Example 05 does it for the agent-loop design.
5e44171aa6:
The ranking is the finding.

The assumptions that swing the monthly value most are the loaded labour rate, the volume and the human minutes per unit: $123k, $114k and $87k. The error rate swings $52k, and the cost per error $34k. The number of calls per unit, the thing everyone argues about, swings $5k.

So when a stakeholder asks whether the agent should make six calls or four, the honest answer is: it hardly matters to the business case. It matters to the latency SLA (next section), which is a constraint in this model, not a variable. The sensitivity result tells you to spend the debate there.

The break-even line answers the architect's question directly. The six-call loop beats the single call only if an error costs more than about $54, against an assumption of $180. If finance says an error costs $30, drop the loop.
0704bf8ba7:
A service level agreement is a promise written in percentiles. If the card says the draft must be ready in 20 seconds at p95, then 95 requests in 100 must finish within 20 seconds. The remaining five may be slower.

For a design with several sequential model calls, you can't add the p95s. The sum of the parts' 95th percentiles overstates the 95th percentile of the sum. And the median of the sum equals the sum of the medians only in symmetric cases. For long-tailed latencies, you must simulate or measure.

The model for one call is simple: time to first token, plus output tokens divided by generation speed, with a long tail on the first term. For several calls in a loop, add the tool time between them.
df7ed769e3: Example 06 simulates five designs with seeded log-normal latencies. The parameters are assumptions, not measurements: a 0.9-second median time to first token, 60 output tokens per second, and 0.6 seconds per tool call. The structure is the point. Replace them with your own measured p50 and p95 per call from the first week of a probe.
dc328d2240:
Five designs, and the verdict is stark.

A single call that writes 600 tokens lands at a p95 of 15.0 seconds. It fits. A two-call workflow (classify, then draft) lands at 17.7 seconds and fits with 2.3 seconds to spare. The six-call agent loop, the design with the best net value in section 11, lands at 56.7 seconds. It misses the SLA by nearly a factor of three. Cutting each call's output to 120 tokens helps (24.7 seconds), but not enough. The ten-call hard case sits near 92 seconds.

Nothing about the model changed between the rows. Only the number of sequential calls and the tokens written per call did. That's the whole argument for the simplest architecture that works: each added step is a bill paid in the currency of the SLA.
8bd6029c24:
Notice how the decision falls out of the card. The primary pillar is efficiency, but the card also states a 20-second p95, because an agent waits for the draft. Net value ranks the agent loop first and the single call second. The SLA eliminates the loop.

The ROI model and the latency model answer different questions. One ranks the options. The other removes the infeasible ones. Do the elimination first, then rank what remains.

There are real ways to try rescuing the loop:

  • trim output tokens;
  • run independent lookups in parallel;
  • cache the prefix to cut time to first token (check the docs for how caching affects latency);
  • stream, so the agent sees the draft forming.

Each is worth measuring. But streaming doesn't change when the draft is complete. If the card says "ready" and the agent needs all of it, streaming won't buy back the SLA.
bf7ce83a70:
Latency is about one request. Capacity is about all of them at once. Launch days, bill-cycle days and promotion days push volume to a multiple of the average. The card states that multiple (3x here) so the design is sized for it.

There are three different limits, and a common mistake is to answer one with the remedy for another.

The rate limit is per minute: requests per minute and tokens per minute, for your organisation and model. (Check the docs for your tier's current limits.)

The concurrency you need follows Little's law: the in-flight count equals the arrival rate times the time each request spends in the system. Take about 440 drafts in the busiest launch-day hour (0.12 per second). A 15-second draft keeps under two requests in flight. The same arrival rate on a 57-second loop keeps about seven.

The budget cap is a monthly dollar figure. It has nothing to do with the minute-level limits.
cb8cde0830:
Take a hypothetical limit of two million tokens a minute. The agent loop's busiest launch-day hour needs about 631,000, so the minute-level limit doesn't bind here. If it had, the remedy would be a queue or throttle in front of the model, not a smaller model.

The dollar view is the one that binds, and example 04 already flagged it: without caching, the run cost at three times volume is $41,424 against a $25,000 cap.

Two different constraints, two different remedies. Throttle for tokens per minute. Caching and tier choice for dollars. An exam option that fixes a cap problem by "requesting a higher rate limit" has answered the wrong question.
d75dcde959:
The Batch API trades latency for price. You get asynchronous processing with a completion window of up to 24 hours, at a reduced price (about half; check the docs for the current discount and limits). One detail matters a lot for design: there's no multi-turn tool use inside a batch item.

The question is never "is batch cheaper?". It's "is anyone waiting?". Example 08 splits four workloads by that question.
a9a1ae8921:
The nightly churn scan of care transcripts is the biggest saving, at $4,000 a month. It's a transformation-pillar workload, and no human is waiting for it. The fallout drafts, where an agent is waiting, stay real-time at full price. The result: a 35 percent cut in the overall bill, without touching accuracy.

In the exam, the telltale phrase is a workload with a deadline measured in hours or days and no user in the loop. A distractor will offer real-time calls with a bigger rate limit. The right answer batches.
2b7a8d5f88: A model is a promise, and a promise needs a check. Example 15 is the Python version of the Java meter in section 11. It computes cost per business unit from usage records, and alerts when that drifts more than 20 percent above the ROI assumption.
78bd629640:
Week 3 shows the point of the exercise. Someone edited the system prompt, which moved the cache breakpoint. The cached share fell from 70 percent to 5 percent.

Accuracy didn't change. Latency barely changed. Only the invoice did, by 118 percent. And only a cost-per-unit meter catches that in days rather than at month end. That's exactly why cost belongs in observability (chapter 10).
ecc7ce199e:
Model selection is covered in chapter 04. This section covers the economics that come first. Given a threshold and a volume, which tier, or combination of tiers, is the cheapest one that clears every segment?

The rule of thumb: pick the cheapest design that passes the worst segment, measured. Treat cost per call as secondary when labour dwarfs tokens, as section 11 showed.

A cascade is the most common compromise: try the small tier, and escalate to the larger tier when the small tier is unsure. Whether it pays depends on one property you must verify, not assume: the small tier's wrong answers must be less confident than its right ones.
99f2aaf5a2:
Three things to take from the sweep.

First, the cascade at a threshold of 0.80 escalates only 3.2 percent of cases and reaches 98.5 percent accuracy, at a third of the cost of always-mid. That looks like a free lunch. It isn't, quite. It depends on the simulated confidences, where wrong answers were drawn from a lower confidence range than right ones. In production you have to demonstrate that. Model-reported confidence is a self-assessment, so measure its calibration (a reliability table on your own labelled set) before routing on it.

Second, look at the worst-segment column. The catch-all code sits between 86 and 95 percent across the thresholds, and touches the line at only one of them. With 200 cases per code, that's within noise. Routing doesn't rescue a segment the underlying capability can't handle. For that code, leave it manual or improve the prompt and data.

Third, at a threshold of 1.01 the cascade degenerates into a small call followed by a mid call. That's strictly worse than going to the mid tier directly. So watch the escalation rate in production. A drift in the small tier's confidence distribution will quietly turn the cascade into the worst of both worlds.
c44d11e9e0:
For a regulated, high-impact workflow, the architecture that survives review has three zones.

Code owns everything that must behave the same way every time. That means fetching the order, the bill or the device record; eligibility rules; limits; arithmetic, including tax; schema and format validation; and the actual write.

Claude owns what is genuinely linguistic. It reads the customer's email or the agent's notes, works out what is being disputed or what failed, maps it to a bill line or a fallout cause, and drafts the explanation.

A gate sits between a validated proposal and the write. It's automatic below a limit and above a confidence. Otherwise, a person approves.

The zones aren't only about accuracy. They're about blast radius and auditability. The model never holds a credential that can write, and every write traces back to a rule or a person.
3539010978:
Here are four runs of the same flow, with a scripted model.

The first proposal is clean and under the limit, so it's applied. The second has an arithmetic mistake: the model says the credit including 8.25 percent tax is $33.99, when it's $32.48. The validator, which is plain code, catches it. The third is correct but over the $50 limit, so it goes to the approval queue. It is never applied silently. The fourth invents a bill line (international_pack) that doesn't exist.

Without the validator, two of the four would have posted wrong credits, and one would have posted a credit larger than any automatic limit. The scripted model is deliberately unreliable. The architecture is what makes that tolerable.

Take one precise claim into the exam: do not ask the model to be right about things code can check.
06258e0b89: On the Spring side, the validator is a pure function with a unit test. The gate is a domain service. It persists its decision with the proposal and the validator's verdict, plus who approved and when, if a person did. That record is exactly what a SOX auditor asks for.
e341d3b693:
The card says 95 percent in every code, and section 10 showed what proving that costs. The practical consequence is a launch plan that treats each segment separately, with three outcomes instead of two.

A segment is GO when the lower bound of its interval clears the threshold. Launch automated drafts.

It's HOLD when the point estimate clears but the interval doesn't. Run it in shadow mode until the interval clears. In shadow mode, Claude drafts, but the agent works as today, and only the comparison is recorded.

It's NO-GO when the point estimate itself is below the line. The segment stays manual while the prompt, the data or the design improves.

Example 11 applies the rule to 400 validation cases per code for the mid tier.
7fe0f5bf65:
Twelve of fourteen codes are GO, covering 97.6 percent of volume.

PROMO_ELIG is a HOLD: 96.8 percent observed, lower bound 0.945. One more month of shadow data will probably settle it, one way or the other. OTHER, the catch-all, is a NO-GO at 91.2 percent, and it covers just 0.4 percent of volume. The sensible call is to leave it manual and not spend a quarter on it.

This is the exam's "measure per type, fix any type below 95 percent before launch" turned into a plan, with one refinement a professional would add: launching is not all-or-nothing. Almost all the value sits in the twelve codes that are ready now.
67a4e6aacb: Before the first automated draft, the ROI model's inputs are guesses: the draft error rate, the minutes agents will spend with a draft, the share of drafts they edit. Shadow mode measures them on production traffic, without exposing customers. Example 14 analyses a synthetic shadow log.
92db1c24b1:
Three things come out.

First, two guessed inputs get replaced by measurements: human minutes per unit (2.86) and the draft error rate (1.63 percent, which includes the weak codes). Rerun section 11 with them, and the case either holds or it doesn't.

Second, the edit rate on correct drafts (roughly 14 percent here) is a style cost, not an accuracy cost. Track it separately, so a rise in edits isn't misread as a rise in errors.

Third, only eight of fourteen codes are ready by the strict interval rule at this sample size. They cover 90 percent of volume, lower than the 97.6 percent the larger validation set gave. Sample size again: a code with 72 shadow tickets can't prove 95 percent. That's information, not a failure.
507e89502a:
Architects rarely get one use case. They get a backlog from five business units. The same card and the same ROI model rank them.

Score each candidate on four things: value (monthly net from the ROI model), feasibility (worst-segment probe result, data availability), risk (impact of a wrong output, compliance burden) and time to first value.

Prefer high-value, high-feasibility, moderate-risk items. They produce a measured win that funds the harder ones. They also build the shared platform (gateway, evaluation harness, trace store, cost meter) that every later use case reuses.

Apply the fit test to every candidate. In the scoring below, a non-LLM alternative halves the case for Claude.
05183994f0:
The ranking is stable where it matters. The care-transcript churn scan (batch, low risk, transformation) comes first under both weightings. The retail receipt-dispute triage is second.

Autonomous plan changes look valuable at $250k. But they sit fourth under a value-weighted view and last under a risk-weighted one. A 0.88 probe on a billing and CPNI action is not a candidate for autonomy. The "draft and approve" variant is a different, lower-risk project, and it should be scored separately.

The store-hours chatbot and the invoice extraction both carry a non-LLM alternative, so they drop. When changing the weights reorders the top three, the ADR should say why. When it only reorders the bottom, nobody needs to care.
31c0ac4e83: Every decision in this chapter is a trade-off with a number on each side. The table below lists the ones the exam keeps coming back to, with the quantity that decides each. Memorise the right-hand column, not the left.
06090dc436:
The anti-patterns below are the same decisions, made badly. In each, the broken version is code that looks reasonable in a pull request, and the fix is a few lines.

Keep a mental picture of the broken code. It helps in the exam, because the distractor options almost always describe it.
cc23e776c4:
The output of this chapter is a decision. A decision that lives only in a meeting gets re-argued in the next one.

The architecture decision record (ADR) is the artefact that stops that. Because the card holds the numbers, the ADR can be generated from it. Example 17 produces a draft from card.json and the models in this chapter.
ecc35010b4:
Look at what the ADR does that a slide doesn't.

It states the context, with its source and date range. It states the decision as a structure (what code does, what Claude does, what a person does), not as "use an agent". It states the consequences as numbers, including the modelled p95 against the SLA.

And it lists the alternatives rejected, each with the reason that eliminated it. The six-call loop is rejected for p95, not for quality. The cascade is deferred, pending shadow data. Six months later, when someone proposes the six-call loop again, the record answers the objection before the meeting starts.
d033135d3d:
The conversation with stakeholders follows the same structure, in a different order. Lead with the decision this audience cares about. Give the two or three numbers that justify it. Name what you're trading away.

To the sponsor: twelve of fourteen fallout codes go live in the first release, covering 97.6 percent of volume. The model predicts a payback of about 1.5 months at placeholder prices. One code waits in shadow mode, and one stays manual.

To finance: net $217k a month, sensitive mostly to labour rate and volume. The break-even cost per error is far below the assumed value. A monthly cost meter alerts at 20 percent over.

To security and compliance: the model never holds a write credential. Every write is validated by code, and approved by a person, or by a rule under a limit. Data classes and residency are on the card.

To the operations lead: agents see a draft in about 15 seconds, and edit or accept it. Their edits feed the weekly evaluation set.

Chapter 15 covers how to run these conversations, and chapter 16 how to keep the numbers current after launch. The point here is simpler. Each audience asks about a different line of the card, so the card is also the agenda.
c85fd7fc9f:
One more habit of professionals: say what you don't know. If finance gives the cost per error as a range of $90 to $300, show the sensitivity result and the break-even. If prices are placeholders, say so, and give the date you'll replace them.

Calibrated honesty is the most reliable way to keep a business case alive through its first review.
5af9af3bc1:
CCAR-P scenarios give you figures and four plausible designs. Here is the method that works:

(1) Find the primary pillar. (2) List the hard constraints: SLA, compliance, per-segment threshold, cap. (3) Eliminate every option that violates one. (4) Among what remains, prefer the simplest design, and the one justified by a measurement.

Work each scenario before you open the answer. Real exam items will be worded differently, so treat these as practice for the reasoning. Check the official exam guide for the current format.
aafc6e02f0:
A contract-analysis assistant for a carrier's legal department is tested on 600 labelled clauses. Overall accuracy is 96 percent.

The requirement is 95 percent for each of six contract types, and 96 percent overall. Four types are at 97 to 99 percent. Indemnification clauses are at 91 percent (n = 110). Limitation-of-liability clauses are at 94 percent (n = 90).

The sponsor wants to launch all six next month. What do you recommend?
c77429649d:
The requirement is written per type, so an overall pass doesn't satisfy it. Option A is the aggregate-gate anti-pattern.

B applies the requirement as written, and adds the interval check. With n of 90 to 110 per type, a point estimate of 97 percent has a lower bound near 0.92. So "four types pass" needs larger-n confirmation, or shadow mode, before those types are called GO.

C changes the model without measuring. A larger tier can improve one clause type and not another, and the only way to know is to measure per type. D rewrites the requirement to fit the result. That's a stakeholder decision, made in the open with the risk stated, not an engineering shortcut.

The phrase to remember: measure per type, fix any type below 95 percent before launch.
57e54a738a:
A live-agent desktop needs a suggested reply within 10 seconds at p95. The primary pillar is the performance SLA.

Design A makes one call: $0.02 per case, p95 4 s, 93 percent acceptable drafts. Design B is a four-step agent: $0.30 per case, p95 25 s, 94 percent acceptable drafts. The acceptance threshold is 90 percent.

Which do you choose?
5b11f9fb7e:
An SLA is a constraint, not a weight.

Design B's modelled p95 is 2.5 times the limit, and throughput can't repair it. A rate limit governs how many requests per minute you may send, not how long one request takes. So option C answers the wrong question.

A meets both the SLA and the 90 percent threshold, and it costs $0.28 less per case. At 100,000 cases a month, that's $28,000. Option D adds cost and complexity to cover a problem A already solves. Accuracy beyond the threshold is no reason to break the primary pillar.
4130dc35ab:
A retailer processes 18,000 returns a month. Agents spend 6 minutes on each, at a loaded $0.60 a minute. About 2.2 percent are fraudulent, and an approved fraudulent return costs $140.

A proposal lets Claude auto-approve returns under $75, cutting agent time on those to 1 minute. In a shadow test on 1,200 historical under-$75 returns, the human decision caught 31 fraudulent returns. Claude's recommendation would have let 6 of those through.

Which action is best?
6496bc397a: Compute the break-even. Auto-approval saves 5 minutes times $0.60 = $3.00 per return. Each extra leaked fraud costs $140, so the break-even added leakage is about 2.1 percent of returns. Claude's observed added leakage is 0.5 percent ($0.70 per return). So auto-approve under $75, with a monitored leakage alert and sampled audits, and keep human review above $75.
4729d8d41c:
This is the cost-of-error argument, with numbers.

Labour saved is $3.00 per return. Added leakage costs 0.005 times $140 = $0.70. So the net is about $2.30 per return: roughly $41,000 a month if every return were under $75 (scale it by the actual share). The break-even is $3.00 divided by $140, about 2.1 points of leakage.

The observed 0.5 percent rests on only 31 fraud cases, so its interval is wide. The sensible launch therefore includes a leakage alert and audits, and the decision gets revisited as data builds up.

A treats the number as certain. B ignores that the status quo also lets some fraud through, and rejects a positive-value change without doing the arithmetic. D extends automation into the band where errors cost more and there's no evidence.
af05dc1728:
A carrier wants Claude to answer plan-change questions, including the prorated charge for a mid-cycle upgrade. The proration rules are published and fixed. Today, wrong prorations cause 40 percent of billing complaints about plan changes.

Which design is best?
588da744c4: Put the proration in a code function (inputs: plan prices, cycle dates, change date) and expose it as a tool. Claude extracts the parameters from the conversation, calls the tool and explains the result. The unit-tested function is the only source of the number.
a43bb94f14:
The logic is fully specified, so it belongs in code. Code is exact, auditable, and costs nothing per call. Claude's job is language: understanding the request and explaining the figure.

A and D keep the arithmetic probabilistic, and pay for it twice: in tokens, and in an error rate that never reaches zero. Majority voting reduces random errors, but it doesn't make arithmetic exact. B is both expensive and unnecessary for rules you can write down.

The fit test says it plainly: structured logic means code.
6ef7d906c2:
A new fallout code has 0.8 percent of volume. The team's test set has 40 labelled cases, and Claude got all 40 right. The requirement is 95 percent per code.

The team proposes launching this code with automated drafts today. What's the best response?
1b9f0684e9: Don't claim the threshold is met. 40 clean cases can't show 95 percent at the usual confidence; about 59 clean cases are needed. Run the code in shadow mode until the evidence builds up, or label more cases. At 0.8 percent of 41,000 (about 330 a month), reaching 59 cases takes roughly two more months of shadow traffic, or less if historical tickets can be labelled.
a8d2163a5e:
Forty clean cases give a Wilson lower bound near 0.91, which is below the threshold. And the exact-binomial minimum for zero failures is 59 (example 13).

The code is small, so shadow mode builds evidence quickly, at little risk. The chapter's three-state rule calls it HOLD, not GO.

A reads a point estimate as proof. C changes the taxonomy to hide the problem. D tunes a different knob, and doesn't address the evidence at all.
0b0ece302c:
A design costs about $18,000 in an average month, fixed operations included. The card sets a $25,000 monthly cap. Two launch days a month run at three times normal daily volume.

The team lead proposes switching to a smaller model tier "to be safe" and requesting a higher rate limit. What's the right assessment?
536d6ce834: Compute it. Say token spend is the variable part, averaging $12,000 of the $18,000. Two days at triple volume add about 2 x 2 x $12,000 / 30 = $1,600, for a total of about $19,600: under the cap. A tier change and a limit increase aren't needed until measurements show a rate-limit error or a trend towards the cap. Keep the cost meter, with an alert at 85 percent of the cap.
7a3efc74ab:
The cap is monthly and the peaks last two days. The arithmetic shows the headroom.

Switching tier to guard against a problem the numbers don't show puts per-segment accuracy at risk, and per-segment accuracy is the constraint that chose the tier in the first place. Batch (C) is only right where nobody is waiting, and an agent waiting for a draft is waiting. D is a financing choice, not a design response.

The rate limit is a separate question. It's answered by tokens per minute at the busiest hour, not by the monthly total.
7bc7e30c43:
Done when: you can explain why each example's output leads to its decision, and the card for your own process lints clean, with assumptions labelled. You should also be able to state, for your process:

  • the primary pillar;
  • the worst-segment accuracy;
  • the modelled p95 against the SLA;
  • the monthly cost at peak against the cap;
  • the break-even cost per error.

If you can, you're ready for chapter 02.
